title: Winter Wonderland returns to downtown Caldwell, drawing families from across the Treasure Valley
summary: After months of preparation, downtown Caldwell is glowing once again as families from across the Treasure Valley gather for the annual Winter Wonderland Festival.
text:
CALDWELL, Idaho — After months of preparation, downtown Caldwell is glowing once again as families from across the Treasure Valley gather for the annual Winter Wonderland Festival.
The celebration marks the payoff after months of work preparing downtown for the holiday season. Idaho News 6 has followed those preparations, from local businesses getting ready for one of their busiest times of the year to the small crew responsible for stringing lights throughout downtown.
Now, the lights are on and visitors are filling the streets.
WATCH | Winter Wonderland returns, drawing families from across the Treasure Valley
For Ralph Cloud, Winter Wonderland has become a holiday tradition. He said he has been coming to the event since moving to the area in 2018.
“Just all the lights, all the people, the community is so engaging that everybody talks and waves to everybody when you walk past them,” Cloud said. “The lights at night are just phenomenal. We come several times through the season while it's open. It helps encourage the Christmas spirit.”
Winter Wonderland has grown into one of downtown Caldwell's largest annual draws. More than 30,000 people have been known to visit downtown during the festival's three-day opening weekend.
Some of the people filling the streets Friday have been coming since they were children.
“It's a great family event, to be honest,” Robert Johnson said, who was out celebrating the awesome pyrotechnics of the dragon with his 13-year-old son Victor.
“You get a decent walk and it's spread out better than the other ones. It really is. You just meet a lot of people and it's fun," he said.
While some visitors live in Caldwell, others make the trip into town from surrounding communities.
Cloud came in from Greenleaf and said getting out to see the lights and the crowds is part of the experience.
“Greenleaf is nice and being retired, we're pretty much stay at home now anyway, but it's nice to come out every now and then and just see everybody and see the lights,” he said.
The Winter Wonderland Festival continues through the weekend from 5 to 10 p.m. While the opening festival lasts just a few days, the holiday lights will continue illuminating downtown Caldwell into the winter season.

title: US House vote on Veterans Day over contentious TCAVA bill incenses many vets
summary: WASHINGTON — Many military veterans are opposing a U.S. House-passed proposal to revamp retirement and disability benefits, saying it threatens future veterans’ compensation. The House passed two bills last week that address the issue. What’s at stake is whether some 58,000 — and counting — medically retired veterans who suffered combat-related injuries before meeting 20 […]
text:
US House vote on Veterans Day over contentious TCAVA bill incenses many vets
Take Care of America’s Veterans Act cuts future disability support for sleep apnea and tinnitus, as well as raising funding fees on VA home loans
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical campus in Rapid City, South Dakota. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)
WASHINGTON — Many military veterans are opposing a U.S. House-passed proposal to revamp retirement and disability benefits, saying it threatens future veterans’ compensation.
The House passed two bills last week that address the issue. What’s at stake is whether some 58,000 — and counting — medically retired veterans who suffered combat-related injuries before meeting 20 years of service can receive both full disability and full retirement, and who pays for it.
Under current law those medically retired before reaching the 20-year mark do not receive full retirement.
The standalone Major Richard Star Act, which would provide full disability and retirement benefits to veterans who were injured in combat before reaching 20 years of service, passed Nov. 12 in an overwhelming 392-18 vote.
The other measure, a package that combined 60 pieces of veterans-related legislation, passed by voice vote a day earlier, on Veterans Day. That package, titled the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, or TCAVA, includes the Major Richard Star Act.
While the Major Richard Star Act contains no provision for funding the benefits increase, the TCAVA does in the form of cutting future disability support for sleep apnea and tinnitus, as well as raising funding fees on VA home loans.
Sleep apnea and tinnitus are common injuries among veterans who are exposed to repeated loud noises and poor sleep conditions. Tinnitus, or persistent ringing and buzzing when no sound is present, ranked first among all disability compensation recipients in 2025, according to the Veteran Benefits Administration’s annual report.
The TCAVA also combines dozens of provisions meant to streamline some VA infrastructure and health professional credentialing, as well as expand benefits for caregivers and survivors, including allowing survivors who remarry before age 55 to continue to be eligible for benefits, among other measures.
The Major Richard Star Act would cost $13 billion over the next decade, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. The budget office does not have an estimate for TCAVA.
The Senate is only in session for four more weeks in the 119th Congress, and it’s unclear if the Republican-led Senate will take up either bill for a vote. An aide in the office of Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said leadership does not have an update on the bills at this time.
Future cuts?
Several veterans have spoken out against TCAVA, expressing concern that future veterans will have to pay for retirement and disability benefits that current veterans should be entitled to in full.

title: Mitch Wieland Reads “After a Rainstorm” by Robert Wrigley
summary: On the third week of November, Mitch Wieland reads “After a Rainstorm,” a poem by Robert Wrigley.
text:
Before her death in Auschwitz at the age of 29, Etty Hillesum experienced spiritual awakenings even in her darkest days. Hillesum was a writer and thinker, Dutch and Jewish, later known for her letters and journals about time under Nazi occupation in the Netherlands. Her work was finally collected and published in 1981 under the title “An Interrupted Life.” She wrote not of finding ecstasy in external things, but allowing life to happen and finding peace within.
“I know and share the many sorrows a human being can experience, but I do not cling to them,” she wrote. “They pass through me, like life itself, as a broad eternal stream.”
She’d witnessed her entire family’s disappearance - parents and two brothers - all at the hands of the Nazi regime, all later killed. Her final written words were a postcard dropped from a train, thanking those left behind in the ghetto for their “kindness and care.”
“Ultimately, we have just one moral duty,” she’d written the year before. “To reclaim large areas of peace in ourselves, more and more peace, and to reflect it toward others. And the more peace there is in us, the more peace there will also be in our troubled world.”
It’s the third week of November and we’re hearing writing along the theme of reclamation this month. Today, Mitch Wieland shares a poem by Robert Wrigley, titled “After a Rainstorm." A poet and educator with fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts, Wrigley has published over 15 collections of poetry, including his most recent, “A True Account of Myself as a Bird.”
Something I Heard is supported by Idaho Commission on the Arts and the National Endowment for the Arts.

title: Idaho legislators planning regulation of e-motos, issue warning to parents
summary: As the holiday season approaches, Idaho lawmakers have their attention fixed on potentially dangerous gifts for children — e-motos.
text:
BOISE, Idaho — As the holiday season approaches, Idaho lawmakers have their attention fixed on potentially dangerous gifts for children — e-motos.
Representative Brooke Green shared that e-motos are often advertised as e-bikes — but these devices reach speeds of over 30 mph, and aren't street-legal.
According to Green, parents are being urged to reconsider purchasing these devices for children who are not legally able to ride motorcycles on public roads.
The legislation that Green and Senator Treg Bernt plan to bring forward during the 2027 legislative session would propose reclassifying e-motos as motorcycles. This would mean riders would need to get a motorcycle endorsement and ensure their vehicles met street-legal requirements before they could hit the roads.
"Parents should be aware that these vehicles are being marketed as e-bikes, but they are actually high-powered electric motorcycles, many of which are not street-legal. Families are spending thousands of dollars on what they believe are bicycles, without realizing their 14-year-old cannot legally ride them down Eagle Road or on the Greenbelt. Kids are getting seriously hurt, and we need to address this before more injuries occur. There's nothing wrong with enjoying these vehicles in the desert or on our public lands where motorized recreation is permitted, but motorcycles do not belong on the Greenbelt, sidewalks, or other pedestrian spaces. We want parents to have the facts before making  expensive holiday purchases, and we're working on bipartisan legislation to establish clear rules that keep our communities safe." — Senator Treg Bernt and Representative Brooke Green
The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare says that statewide, hospitals have noted over 1,000 e-device-related hospitalizations since July, which raised concerns for legislators and generated urgency around creating safety standards for e-device use.

title: Trump pitches compromise with Democrats on healthcare, immigration
summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump will likely veto many of the bills that Democrats pass once they take control of Congress next year, he said Friday, though he suggested negotiations on healthcare and immigration were possible. “They’re going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send […]
text:
Trump pitches compromise with Democrats on healthcare, immigration
President said he will likely veto many bills the Dem-controlled Congress sends his way next year
President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on August 6, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump will likely veto many of the bills that Democrats pass once they take control of Congress next year, he said Friday, though he suggested negotiations on healthcare and immigration were possible.
“They’re going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “But I think after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ‘I’m going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’”
Trump then referred to House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, both of New York, as “smart” and indicated he would be willing to work with them on some issues.
“There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare. I am open to great healthcare,” he said. “Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.”
Trump said several Democrats have called him in recent weeks, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who he said wanted to discuss border security.
“I received a phone call two days ago from the new governor-elect of Texas. She was really nice. It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border,” he said. “And I think we’ll be able to work something out because that’s a very important thing.”
Must-pass items
Trump and Democratic leaders in Congress will need to negotiate much more than healthcare and immigration once divided government begins in January.
They will need to work out bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual government spending bills that fund scores of departments and agencies as well as the thousands of programs they administer. Failing to accomplish the work, or approving a stopgap spending bill instead, would lead to yet another shutdown.
Congress and the White House will also likely need to negotiate another debt-ceiling increase early next year. Without agreement, the country would default for the first time in modern history, very likely plunging the economy into a tailspin.
Not addressing the debt ceiling before the remainder of the $5 trillion in new borrowing authority approved by Republicans in last year’s “big, beautiful” law expires would limit the federal government to only spend what it brings in.
That would lead to ramifications more significant than a government shutdown, including the possibility that Social Security checks would not go out on time and that medical providers wouldn’t be reimbursed for Medicare or Medicaid patients treatment.

title: Idaho Botanical Garden expansion aims to build community
summary: Earlier this year, the Idaho Botanical Garden nearly doubled in size at its picturesque location nestled at the base of the Boise Foothills.
text:
Earlier this year, the Idaho Botanical Garden nearly doubled in size at its picturesque location nestled at the base of the Boise Foothills.
The 10-acre expansion brings with it an arboretum in its infancy stage. The young trees will eventually grow to tower over visitors and offer much needed shade to the garden.
It also includes a new event lawn and several new gardens showcasing plants that heal us, amaze us or help feed us.
The staff even extended the new experience to the parking lot and new bike pavilion where happy succulents and cacti will poke out from crags in the wall to greet visitors.
James Dawson recently got a tour of the new spaces and brings us this postcard.
Editor's note: The Idaho Botanical Garden is a financial supporter of Boise State Public Radio, but had no involvement with the development or production of this story.
A transcript of the audio tour is available below:
Colin Lyman: So my name is Colin Lyman. I'm the director of horticulture and facilities at Idaho Botanical Garden. So I'm over everything outside: buildings, infrastructure and plants. So we are right below where our old entrance used to be. And we're standing in the the new bike garden. We can fit 177 to 200 bikes in here. There's lots of bike hoops. We have a raised planter beds with seat walls for seating, a bike pavilion, and then we have our rock wall. And in the wall there's little cracks and nooks and crannies that next spring we'll be installing cactus and succulents all the way throughout because there's so much concrete below it. We can the heat from that reflects, and we can create microclimates to grow things that normally wouldn't be able to grow.
Colin Lyman: Right next to the bike garden is the parking garden. We call it a parking garden, because the whole point of it is to be full of plant material, so that when you drive into the garden to park, you feel immersed in the experience when you arrive, and you can feel that, especially right now in the border bed that ligns Old Penitentiary Road. It's very full. Right now, we have some space empty. We're planning more things this fall. Because of the diversity of the plant list, some of the things were difficult to find. To the left of our kiosks is the future home of the Boise Farmers Market. Right now it's a gravel pad, but it's the future site of our events building, education building and an administration building. We looked at event space. What is the event space size that is missing in the Treasure Valley? And that size is between 600 and 800.
Colin Lyman: And so that was important for us to fill that niche and fill that need for the community. We're really big on sense of community here. Partnering with the Boise Farmers Market, I think makes a lot of sense. Like our mission is connecting people, plants, and nature. And what the Boise Farmers Market does is a portion of that.

title: Commentary: Idaho nonprofit Envision provides the gift of sight and hearing
summary: Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss. Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way. “I’ve […]
text:
Idaho nonprofit Envision provides the gift of sight and hearing
Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and demand is high, writes guest columnist Chuck Malloy.
Idaho nonprofit Envision helps provide eye exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. (Photo by Getty Images)
Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss.
Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way.
“I’ve seen people break down and cry when they put on a pair of glasses and discover they are able to see,” Lugo says. “It fills my heart with joy being able to do that – and I sleep well at night knowing that we are making a difference. But it’s not just me. It’s the volunteers and office co-workers who see that happen, and the 1,400 Lions Club members throughout the state who get information about what’s being done. So, a lot of people are involved.”
And Lance Grady of Boise is glad for that. He didn’t break down in tears when he recently was fitted with glasses, but he did look across a street and see a squirrel climbing a tree. And he could see letters, numbers and names on buildings.
“I wouldn’t have been able to see any of that without my glasses,” he said. “This has been life changing. I can drive and do other things that I was unable to do.”
Grady’s story began by word of mouth.
“A family friend talked with me about reaching out to the Lions,” he said. “They were determined to help me find something – without spending $400 for a pair of glasses. “I’m so thankful … a lot of stress has been lifted from me.”
Lugo has seen similar stories play out many times.
“When people are able to see, they can get a driver’s license, fill out a job application and be productive,” Lugo says. “There is such a big gap with healthcare, and we’re only talking about eyesight and hearing. The state doesn’t provide aid with eyeglasses for those over the age of 18, so you are not going to get eyecare assistance if you are at the poverty level.”
Envision helps fill the void, providing exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and Lugo says demand is high.
“I get at least 20 applications in my email box every day, which is about 600 a month,” he says. “Every one of those are from people who need glasses and are at the poverty level. There are a lot of people who are hurting.”
Envision started in 1969 as Idaho’s only eye bank and arranging corneal transplants remain a big part of the nonprofit’s operation – along with the tradition of collecting and refurbishing used eyeglasses. title: Nearly 40% of new Idaho inmates had drug charges, state watchdog report on overcrowded prisons finds
summary: In Idaho, which imprisons women at the highest rate in the nation, drug charges account for much of the state’s prison population, a new watchdog report found. The report by the independent state agency, the Office of Performance Evaluations, highlighted why the state has the seventh-highest incarceration rate in the nation, and the highest in […]
text:
Nearly 40% of new Idaho inmates had drug charges, state watchdog report on overcrowded prisons finds
Idaho has nation’s highest incarceration rate for women. Many are in custody on drug charges, new Office of Performance Evaluations report finds.
There are approximately 8,000 incarcerated individuals in nine state-owned prisons and five community reentry centers across Idaho. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Idaho Capital Sun)
In Idaho, which imprisons women at the highest rate in the nation, drug charges account for much of the state’s prison population, a new watchdog report found.
The report by the independent state agency, the Office of Performance Evaluations, highlighted why the state has the seventh-highest incarceration rate in the nation, and the highest in the Mountain West. Over the past decade, drug possession sentences account for 39% of the state’s prison growth, more than any other crime, the agency’s researchers found.
Researchers said the drug crime data they analyzed didn’t show which drugs people were charged with being in possession of, or of trafficking. But user data they obtained from the state’s drug court system found that methamphetamine was by far the most reported, by 48% of people, with heroin and other opioids in second with 20%.
“While women are less likely than men to be incarcerated for drug possession, they are much less likely to be incarcerated for other crimes,” the report found. “More than half of the growth of women in custody over the past two decades comes from women convicted of a single drug possession charge.”
The 88-page report delivered a slew of statistics, including:
- Twice as many women were imprisoned in Idaho in 2025 than in 2005.
- Women are likely in prison for drug possession, even more than other drug offenses. Over a fifth, 22%, of females in prison in Idaho had just one drug possession sentence, compared to just 10% of males in prison.
- Nearly two thirds, 61%, of women in prisons had drug possession sentences, compared to 35% of men in prisons.
- Drug possession was the least likely category of crimes to have charges amended, with just 6% of felony cases being reduced to misdemeanors or lesser charges. Researchers used 2022 data for that metric to give court cases time to close. Researchers say that statistic can be explained by drug possession laws offering less sentencing options than other crimes, and inconsistencies in access to misdemeanor probation.
As the rest of the nation’s imprisonment rates fell amid declining crime rates, Idaho’s largely didn’t budge, the report found. The state kept incarcerating a similar share of people, even during years of peak population growth and reduced crime rates.
A bipartisan group of state lawmakers requested the study in March to help address the state’s overflowing prisons.
Four of the state’s largest counties — Ada, Canyon, Kootenai and Twin Falls — contributed the bulk, 87%, of growth in the state’s inmate population.

Psychedelic mental healthcare for veterans wins bipartisan backing from US House panel
Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report
The Department of Veterans Affairs in Washington, D.C., on June 22, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
NOTE: This story mentions suicide. If you or a loved one needs help during a mental health crisis, call or text 988, or visit 988helpline.org. Help is available for veterans and nonveterans alike.
WASHINGTON — Federal regulators could be on the cusp of approving psychedelic-assisted mental health treatment for veterans, but lawmakers asked tough questions Wednesday of Trump administration officials over whether the Department of Veterans Affairs can meet patients’ needs, and if federal law enforcement and health agencies are on the same page.
Just over 2 million veterans suffer with treatment-resistant depression, and approximately 180,000 of them would likely meet the criteria for treatment with psychedelic compounds, including MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, DMT and ibogaine, according to the Veterans Health Administration.
Members of the House Committee on Veterans Affairs Subcommittee on Health grilled officials for roughly two and a half hours during an afternoon hearing contemplating how the VA should implement the labor-intensive treatments if given the green light by the Food and Drug Administration.
Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report, published in September.
“Something needs to change,” said subcommittee chair Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who said despite prevention efforts, the numbers have remained “stubbornly stagnant.”
“When I came to Congress in 2021, I didn’t think I’d be sitting here today advocating for these emerging breakthrough therapies, but in meeting with veterans from all walks of life, I have found the effectiveness of these treatments and am willing to advance it as potential hope,” said Miller-Meeks, who recently lost her bid for reelection.
Miller-Meeks, an Army veteran and ophthalmologist, cited randomized clinical trials for MDMA-assisted therapies that commenced this year at VA facilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, both of which resulted from funding allocated in 2024.
Miller-Meeks also praised President Donald Trump’s April executive order directing the FDA to work with other agencies, including the VA, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Department of Health and Human Services to remove barriers, like drug enforcement classification, that complicate testing the treatments.
The possibility of new treatments was met with optimism on both sides of the aisle.
The subcommittee’s ranking member Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., said the clinical trials are “extremely welcome news and will change lives for the better.”

title: Utah lawmakers introduce bills expanding where high-level nuclear waste is allowed
summary: The U.S. Department of Energy hasn’t released its final decision on sites for “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” but Utah, one of the finalists, is preparing its regulatory framework with a set of bills proposed for next legislative session. Fountain Green Republican Sen. Derrin Owens is sponsoring a bill on regional nuclear lifecycle campuses. The draft […]
text:
Utah lawmakers introduce bills expanding where high-level nuclear waste is allowed
The state is a finalist for the US Department of Energy’s Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus proposal
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The U.S. Department of Energy hasn’t released its final decision on sites for “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” but Utah, one of the finalists, is preparing its regulatory framework with a set of bills proposed for next legislative session.
Fountain Green Republican Sen. Derrin Owens is sponsoring a bill on regional nuclear lifecycle campuses. The draft isn’t publicly available yet, but Owens said it will lay out the state’s involvement in safety practices for the site proposed in Tooele County.
Utah currently has strict regulations on high-level spent nuclear fuel waste storage, but has made exceptions for test reactors in state facilities, like the one at the San Rafael Energy Lab. If the bill becomes law, state restrictions on high-level nuclear waste won’t apply to the designated campus zone.
“Before the U.S. Department of Energy can commit to Utah, state law needs to be adjusted and cleared, and limited exceptions for that type of handling of fuel needs to be allowed, or made legal in the state,” Owens told the Public Utilities, Energy and Technology Interim Committee on Wednesday.
Shipments of the material would also need to be allowed, Owens said. But that would need both federal and state legislation.
That exception may also be extended to commercial nuclear reactors under another bill sponsored by Richfield Republican Rep. Carl Albrecht. That draft would also update the high-level waste law in Utah, providing exceptions for nuclear power reactors located in the state and licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, including commercial plants, which currently aren’t allowed to store high-level waste on site.
Meanwhile, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright acknowledged earlier this month that before a nuclear lifecycle campus could take shape, Congress would need to approve a new nuclear waste disposal site.
What would Utah’s campus allow
Owens’ bill would also list activities allowed within the nuclear innovation campus, which, he said, would include advanced nuclear reactors, nuclear fuel fabrication and enrichment, recycling and reprocessing of used nuclear fuel, storage and disposal of nuclear material, and medical and industrial isotope production, as well as research, manufacturing, workforce training, and the needed infrastructure to support all of those activities.
The campus impact could be comparable to 10 times that of Kennecott’s copper mine, “if you did some weird math,” Owens told the committee. “So we are approaching this strategically and carefully and slowly and trying to get it right.”

title: Bird flu outbreak in Washington state dairies is linked to virus transmitted from Idaho
summary: The ongoing bird flu outbreak in Washington state dairies, which has resulted in the death of a dairy worker, likely originated from Idaho cattle, according to federal officials. The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced this month that an analysis of genetic sequencing indicated the virus that has infected Washington dairy herds and workers likely came […]
text:
Bird flu outbreak in Washington state dairies is linked to virus transmitted from Idaho
Virus has been detected in Idaho dairies since 2024; Washington dairy worker dies amid outbreak
Milking cows at an Idaho dairy on July 20, 2012. Highly pathogenic avian influenza, known as bird flu, has been detected in some Idaho dairies since 2024. A recent outbreak in Washington state dairies was determined to have likely come to the state from Idaho through cattle movement. (Photo by Kirsten Strough/USDA)
The ongoing bird flu outbreak in Washington state dairies, which has resulted in the death of a dairy worker, likely originated from Idaho cattle, according to federal officials.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced this month that an analysis of genetic sequencing indicated the virus that has infected Washington dairy herds and workers likely came from Idaho through cattle movement.
New bird flu cases appear in dairy herds as state ag, vet officials seek vaccine urgency
Earlier this month, a Yakima County farmworker in Washington died after contracting the virus, the Washington State Standard reported. The person had underlying health conditions and became ill after exposure to an infected dairy animal, according to the Yakima Health District.
USDA spokesperson Tanya Espinosa told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that officials can’t determine the date of transmission through genetic sequencing. She said that “Idaho is aware” that the analysis indicated the virus originated in the Gem State.
A spokesperson from Idaho State Department of Agriculture told the Sun the state agency has continued its response to bird flu detection for more than two years.
“Throughout this time, the department has actively conducted surveillance, monitoring and testing efforts to track the disease and protect Idaho’s livestock industry,” ISDA spokesperson Elizabeth Fisher said in an email. “ISDA has aggressively and consistently pursued outreach and education to producers as to the importance of continued testing and monitoring for HPAI on their facilities since the disease was first detected in the state.”
Idaho reported its first detection in dairy cattle of highly pathogenic avian influenza, known as bird flu, in April 2024. Since then, there have been 180 reported cases of the virus detected in Idaho livestock, according to the USDA.
Two of the confirmed cases were reported in the last 30 days, the USDA case tracker shows. As of Nov. 17, there are 21 dairy facilities in Idaho under quarantine after a detection of the virus, according to the Idaho Department of Agriculture.

title: Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services
summary: Idaho health officials are hoping to increase the pay rate for disability caregivers by 13% next year. The raise request — detailed in the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s budget proposal submitted to the Idaho governor in September — would bring the pay for personal care service workers up to $27.64 per hour. That’s […]
text:
Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services
After budget cuts across state government, Idaho’s Medicaid officials are pursuing a mostly barebones budget — with a few exceptions
Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest budget cuts to the state’s Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor’s State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho health officials are hoping to increase the pay rate for disability caregivers by 13% next year.
The raise request — detailed in the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s budget proposal submitted to the Idaho governor in September — would bring the pay for personal care service workers up to $27.64 per hour. That’s up from Idaho’s current hourly pay rate of $24.44.
That could bring the state out of its status as the lowest paying state for the industry in the Northwest for the first time in years. Idaho has, for years, had a shortage of disability caregivers, who often work in low-paid, demanding jobs.
On the heels of the 2026 legislative session’s deep budget cuts across state government, the request to increase the pay of disability caregivers represents a rare departure from the governor’s office’s instructions for state agencies to continue submitting barebones budgets.
The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare is calling for the pay increase after recently learning that few caregiving agencies can take new patients, Medicaid Administrator Sasha O’Connell said in an interview last month. Through the research, required by federal regulators as part of the state’s recent cuts to doctor pay rates, the state found — by hiring a secret shopper — that only three personal care service agencies, out of 152 across the state, could take children. Less than a third said they could take new adult Medicaid clients.
“What we found is very concerning,” O’Connell said.
The budget request is only one of the first stops for a change in the state’s budget.
Gov. Brad Little will next lay out his priorities for state agencies and the state budget during January’s State of the State Address. But it is ultimately up to the Idaho Legislature to set the state budget and weigh which individual requests make the cut.
Across the board, the raises for disability caregivers would cost the state roughly $3.9 million, and the federal government about $8.1 million. That represents a small chunk of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s overall $6.58 billion budget for next fiscal year, which starts in June. The total budget could see about a 2% increase from what lawmakers approved this fiscal year.
